answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine Hume line — it appears in Section I of his ‘An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding’ (1748), “Of the Different Species of Philosophy,” closing the passage in which Nature counsels a mixed life (Section I then continues for several more paragraphs). The wording is confirmed verbatim against the primary text; the only common variation is ‘amid’ substituted for Hume’s ‘amidst.’

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Section I — “Of the Different Species of Philosophy”

source.excerpt: Indulge your passion for science, says she, but let your science be human, and such as may have a direct reference to action and society. Abstruse thought and profound researches I prohibit, and will severely punish, by the pensive melancholy which they introduce, by the endless uncertainty in which they involve you… Be a philosopher; but, amidst all your philosophy, be still a man.
trail: The line appears in Section I of Hume’s An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, closing the passage in which Nature counsels a mixed life, confirmed verbatim in the primary text.
The work was first published in 1748; the sentence has stood unchanged through every subsequent edition of the ‘Enquiry’.
Popular quote sites such as Goodreads credit it correctly to Hume and to this work.
source.excerptNote: Hume voices Nature herself counselling a “mixed kind of life” — the sentence is the closing exhortation of that passage.

author.name: David Hume
author.heading: About David Hume
author.bio: David Hume was a central figure of the Scottish Enlightenment, best known for his empiricist and skeptical philosophy of mind, causation and religion. His ‘An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding’ (1748) reworked ideas from his earlier ‘A Treatise of Human Nature’ into a more accessible form. The line captures a recurring Humean theme: that philosophy should serve, not supplant, ordinary human life.

misattribution.heading: A note on wording
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is correct — this really is Hume. The only thing worth flagging is a small, widespread wording drift.

items.why: Many reprints and quote sites render it “be a philosopher, but amid all your philosophy be still a man.” Hume’s 1748 text reads ‘amidst’, as confirmed in the Project Gutenberg edition.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Hume’s own, from Section I of the Enquiry — a correct attribution with only a minor ‘amid/amidst’ variant in circulation.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The sentence caps a passage in which Hume has Nature herself scold the over-abstract thinker: pursue knowledge, yes, but keep it “human, and such as may have a direct reference to action and society.” It is Hume’s case for a ‘mixed’ life — reflection tempered by ordinary living.

Detached from that setting, the line reads as a tidy self-help maxim, but in context it is a considered position: philosophy that forgets the human being who philosophizes is, for Hume, a philosophy gone wrong.
